builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
summary: Delta Residue Attribution replaces reading raw patch size as a proxy for over-editing: it replays agent trajectories, attributes each patch unit to the step that wrote it, reverts units individually, and reruns task tests to label code as needed or unneeded; the same protocol can prune agent patches at the harness level using only tests visible to the agent. The cost is substantial compute and engineering, since every unit must be reverted and tests rerun per unit, plus maintaining trajectory replay infrastructure; self-audit prompting is cheaper but weaker (36% recall, 66% precision). What can fail: test-based pruning removes some needed code (46% precision), roughly 11% of pruned patches stop resolving the task, test coverage limits what 'needed' means, and code necessity is negatively correlated with resolve rate on DeepSWE, so optimizing for clean patches may hurt task success.
rationale: The paper contributes an evaluation and post-hoc pruning method rather than a deployable efficiency gain, and its pruning trades a meaningful loss of needed code (46% precision) against cleaner diffs, so the reader should validate it on their own agent workload before relying on it in production.
technique: Trajectory-replay attribution of unneeded patch edits

claims.statement: Delta Residue Attribution replaces reading raw patch size as a proxy for over-editing: it replays agent trajectories, attributes each patch unit to the step that wrote it, reverts units individually, and reruns task tests to label code as needed or unneeded; the same protocol can prune agent patches at the harness level using only tests visible to the agent. The cost is substantial compute and engineering, since every unit must be reverted and tests rerun per unit, plus maintaining trajectory replay infrastructure; self-audit prompting is cheaper but weaker (36% recall, 66% precision). What can fail: test-based pruning removes some needed code (46% precision), roughly 11% of pruned patches stop resolving the task, test coverage limits what 'needed' means, and code necessity is negatively correlated with resolve rate on DeepSWE, so optimizing for clean patches may hurt task success.

Agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean NP_code 0.887 vs 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified); test-based DRA pruning removes most unneeded code at 67% recall and 46% precision, with 89% of pruned patches still resolving the task; no multiplicative speed, memory, or cost improvement is claimed.
